messages.content: I want to characterize bounds for dynamic treatment-regime effects when unmeasured time-varying confounding and informative dropout are both present. The bounds should be sharp under explicit, separately interpretable sensitivity constraints for confounding and dropout. I also want confidence regions with at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly over the specified sensitivity class.

This is a partial-identification goal: the sensitivity constraints define which explanations of the observed information remain admissible, and the resulting range characterizes the dynamic treatment-regime effect across those explanations. Both sources of uncertainty need to be allowed simultaneously. The confounding constraint addresses what may be hidden in treatment decisions over time; the dropout constraint addresses what may be hidden because observation ends informatively. Keeping the constraints separately interpretable makes clear what each permits, even though their implications for the effect may interact.
What exactly would make the bounds sharp?

Sharpness means more than containing every effect value allowed by the assumptions. The bounds should give the tightest range implied by the observed information and the stated sensitivity constraints. In conceptual terms, you consider all admissible explanations consistent with both, then find the lowest and highest possible values of the effect. Values outside that range are ruled out; values within the resulting identified range cannot be ruled out on those grounds alone. Whether an endpoint itself is attained or only approached depends on the formulation, but a loose outer bound would not establish sharp identification.
Does having separate constraints mean I can handle confounding and dropout one at a time?

Not necessarily. “Separately interpretable” describes how each sensitivity restriction is stated and understood. It does not imply that the two mechanisms are independent, that their effects on the bounds are additive, or that combining two separate analyses gives the sharp bounds when both operate. The admissible possibilities must satisfy the confounding and dropout constraints together.
How should I read the word dynamic here?

It refers to treatment regimes whose prescribed actions can depend on information available over time, rather than only to a single fixed treatment choice. The goal concerns effects of those regimes under the two simultaneous identification challenges. It does not, by itself, specify particular regimes, decision times, outcomes, or an effect contrast.
What does informative dropout add to the identification problem?

It means that the loss of observation cannot simply be treated as harmless for learning the effect. A dropout sensitivity constraint limits the ways unobserved information after dropout may differ from what is observed. That limit is distinct from the constraint on unmeasured time-varying confounding, which concerns information relevant to treatment choices and outcomes. Both restrictions have to be reflected in the range of effects considered possible.
If I made one sensitivity constraint less restrictive, should the bounds always widen?

If “less restrictive” means the admissible set is genuinely enlarged while everything else stays fixed, the sharp identified range cannot become narrower: it may widen or stay the same. That is a general consequence of taking extrema over a larger set, not a claim about any particular sensitivity parameter or a promise that changing one constraint will have a visible effect.
And what is the confidence-region requirement asking for beyond the identification bounds?

The bounds describe what is identified under the sensitivity class; a confidence region also accounts for sampling uncertainty in learning from data. The requirement is to construct regions with asymptotic coverage of at least 95%, uniformly over the specified sensitivity class. Thus the guarantee must hold across that class in the asymptotic sense, rather than merely at each fixed admissible case considered in isolation.
So a method that has 95% asymptotic coverage at each individual case might still fall short?

Yes. Pointwise asymptotic coverage does not alone establish a uniform guarantee: the approximation could deteriorate along admissible cases that vary with sample size. The requested property rules out relying solely on a separate limiting statement for every fixed case. The precise coverage statement also needs to identify its inferential target consistently with the effect and its identification bounds; the goal does not prescribe a particular construction.
Can you restate the full aim without choosing a sensitivity model or inference method yet?

Characterize the sharp identification bounds for dynamic treatment-regime effects when unmeasured time-varying confounding and informative dropout occur simultaneously, using explicit sensitivity constraints that can be interpreted separately for the two problems. Then construct confidence regions for the stated inferential target that attain at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly over the specified sensitivity class. This states the required identification and inference properties without choosing particular constraint formulas or a confidence-region procedure.

For the bounds, could we optimize regime values over finite-history latent-response-type polytopes, with separate odds-ratio limits for confounding and dropout, and then project 95% multinomial confidence sets for inference?

That is a concrete proposal for pursuing both parts of the goal. The finite-history latent-response-type representation would describe candidate explanations of the observed information. Separate confounding and dropout odds-ratio limits would restrict those candidates along two interpretable dimensions. Optimizing the regime values over the candidates would produce proposed identification bounds, while projecting a 95% multinomial confidence set would carry uncertainty in the observed probabilities through to the reported region. The sharpness and uniform-coverage claims would still need to be established.
What role do the latent response types play?

They provide a way to represent possible underlying histories and responses that need not be fully observed. In the proposed finite-history formulation, a candidate distribution over those types must agree with the observed information and satisfy the sensitivity restrictions. The regime value is evaluated for each admissible candidate, so optimization asks how low or high it can be under the joint restrictions. This explains the proposed representation; it does not yet establish that a particular representation captures every admissible explanation.
Why specify finite histories?

The proposal is framed around finite histories so that candidate response types and their probabilities can be represented within a finite-dimensional optimization problem. That is the scope stated for this approach. It does not, on its own, claim a result for arbitrary histories or specify how finely histories must be defined.
What does optimizing over a polytope buy us?

It gives a defined feasible set over which to seek extrema of the regime value. If the feasible set exactly represents all and only the explanations permitted by the observed information and both sensitivity limits, its extrema can yield sharp bounds. If it is merely a relaxation or excludes permissible explanations, optimization alone would not establish sharpness. Calling the representation a polytope is part of the proposed formulation; the precise constraints would have to support that formulation.
Could I interpret the two odds-ratio limits as a single allowance for hidden bias?

The proposal instead calls for separate limits: one for unmeasured time-varying confounding and one for informative dropout. An odds-ratio limit provides a way to express how strongly the relevant mechanism may depart from its reference condition, but no numerical limits or exact odds ratios have been specified here. Separate interpretation does not mean separate optimization—the candidate explanations must meet both limits at once.
Would this just mean calculating a bound under confounding and another under dropout, then combining them?

No. The proposed optimization is over a joint set of latent-response-type distributions satisfying both restrictions simultaneously. Separate limits make the assumptions distinguishable; they do not imply that separately calculated bounds can be combined to obtain the joint sharp bound.
How does a treatment regime enter the optimization?

A regime determines the value being evaluated for each admissible candidate explanation. The optimization then takes the lowest and highest compatible values for the effect of interest. Because the goal concerns dynamic treatment-regime effects, the regime can depend on history; the proposal does not specify a particular regime, contrast, or formula for its value.
And what exactly gets projected for the confidence region?

The proposal is to start with a 95% multinomial confidence set for the observed probabilities and project it through the admissible latent-response-type and regime-value calculations. Conceptually, one retains effect values compatible with at least one observed-probability vector in that confidence set and with both sensitivity limits. Projection accounts for uncertainty about the observed probabilities without selecting just a single estimated vector.
Does the 95% label on the multinomial set immediately give the required uniform coverage?

Not automatically. A coverage argument would need the multinomial set to have the requisite coverage across the specified sensitivity class, and the projection to retain the target whenever the relevant observed probabilities are covered. To meet the goal, the resulting confidence regions need at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly over that class. The proposed projection is a route toward that property, not yet a proof of it.
So there are two different questions about whether this proposal works?

Yes. For identification, the question is whether the joint finite-history feasible set—with its separate confounding and dropout odds-ratio limits—exactly captures the possibilities allowed by the assumptions, so that optimizing gives sharp bounds. For inference, the question is whether projecting the 95% multinomial confidence sets yields confidence regions with at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly over the specified sensitivity class. Neither property follows solely from naming the optimization or the confidence set.
How can confounding and dropout odds-ratio limits handle zero-probability histories without sacrificing sharpness or uniform coverage?

That is a key question for the proposed approach. An odds ratio expressed through conditional probabilities may be undefined when a conditioning history has probability zero. A finite-history formulation therefore needs an explicit rule for such histories, rather than silently dividing by zero. The rule must be applied to both the confounding and dropout limits, and the sharpness and coverage arguments must use that same rule.
Why not just impose each odds-ratio limit wherever its conditional probability is defined?

That is one possible starting point. It leaves a further question, though: what happens to candidate explanations at unsupported histories, and to sequences of positive-probability histories approaching zero? If the optimization treats an undefined ratio as unrestricted, excludes the candidate entirely, or applies a limiting restriction, those choices can produce different feasible sets. Sharpness has to be assessed relative to the precise choice, not to an informal odds-ratio statement.
Could the polytope avoid ratios by writing the restrictions without denominators?

Potentially, but that requires care. On histories where all relevant denominators are positive, an odds-ratio inequality may be rewritten in a denominator-free form. At zero-probability histories, the rewritten inequality needs to be checked against the intended interpretation of the original restriction. It might impose a meaningful boundary condition, become vacuous, or admit boundary candidates that the intended model would exclude. An algebraically convenient expression is not, by itself, a proof that the feasible polytope is exact.
If a history has zero probability, doesn't its conditional behavior simply not matter?

A conditional distribution given an event of probability zero is not determined by that event's probability. But for this proposal, the relevant question is broader: whether the proposed latent-response-type representation uses choices at that history when evaluating a regime value, and whether those choices are constrained by the stated sensitivity class. One cannot conclude from the zero probability alone that every assignment there is harmless. The model needs to say what is admissible, and the optimization needs to reflect that decision exactly.
Would it be simpler to require every relevant history to have positive probability?

That would make the conditional odds ratios easier to state, but it would change the class under consideration by excluding zero-probability histories. It also would not by itself address probabilities that approach zero across the class, which can matter for a uniform asymptotic claim. If positivity is used, its scope—and whether a quantitative lower bound is required—would have to be stated as an assumption rather than introduced implicitly to make the formulas work.
So sharpness at the boundary is really about whether the feasible set matches the assumptions?

Exactly. For the proposed optimization to give sharp bounds, its candidate distributions must include every explanation allowed by the observed information and both odds-ratio limits, without including explanations those limits rule out. That matching has to hold when histories have zero probability as well as when they have positive probability. Otherwise the extrema may be bounds for a different sensitivity class.
How do zero-probability histories affect the confidence-region part?

They matter because uniform coverage includes the boundary cases permitted by the specified sensitivity class, not just conveniently interior cases. A confidence-set construction whose justification assumes positive cell probabilities may not automatically have the claimed behavior when a multinomial cell probability is zero or approaches zero. The proposed projection needs a coverage argument for the multinomial set over the relevant class, together with an argument that the projection preserves coverage of its stated target under the same boundary convention used for identification.
Would a zero count in the sample be treated the same way as a zero-probability history?

No. A zero observed count can occur even when the corresponding population probability is positive. A zero-probability history is a feature of a candidate population distribution. The multinomial confidence set is meant to account for uncertainty about such probabilities, so replacing every zero count by a structural zero would risk excluding admissible possibilities. Conversely, the sensitivity constraints still need a defined interpretation if a candidate probability is actually zero.
Could I claim uniform coverage once the projected set covers each fixed probability distribution asymptotically?

Not on that basis alone. Pointwise asymptotic coverage can leave open what happens along sequences of admissible distributions with probabilities tending toward zero. The requested guarantee is at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly over the specified sensitivity class. Its proof must address those sequences if they belong to the class, or explicitly define a class that excludes them; neither can be settled by a pointwise argument alone.
What is the cleanest way to frame the unresolved issue, then?

Specify exactly how each of the separate confounding and dropout odds-ratio limits applies on positive-probability histories and what admissibility means at zero-probability histories. Then ask whether the finite-history latent-response-type optimization represents precisely that joint class, including its boundary, and whether projecting the proposed 95% multinomial confidence sets gives at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly over it. Those are the sharpness and inference questions that the zero-probability case makes especially important.

Here is a hypothesis for the zero-probability issue: closed cross-product constraints for the separate confounding and dropout odds-ratio limits, followed by exact-binomial Bonferroni projection, yield sharp bounds and at least 95% uniform coverage, including zero-probability histories. Does that formulation address the difficulty?

It offers a specific way to address it, but the sharpness and coverage statements remain hypotheses to establish. Cross-product constraints can express odds-ratio limits without requiring division by a probability that might be zero. Making those constraints closed also gives an explicit rule at the boundary. The key identification question is whether that rule describes exactly the intended sensitivity class—including zero-probability histories—rather than a larger or smaller one. The separate inference question is whether the exact-binomial Bonferroni set and its projection provide the stated uniform coverage.
What does “closed” contribute beyond avoiding division by zero?

It specifies that boundary distributions satisfying the cross-product inequalities remain in the feasible set. That can make the behavior of the proposed constraints well defined as probabilities approach zero. But closure is not automatically the right substantive interpretation of an odds-ratio limit: it has to be part of the sensitivity class being claimed. Otherwise a boundary distribution admitted by the closed constraint might not be admissible under the intended assumption.
So even if the constraints work whenever the odds ratios are defined, sharpness at zero still needs an argument?

Yes. Equivalence at positive-probability histories is only part of it. For sharpness, the feasible distributions specified by the closed cross-product constraints must coincide with all distributions allowed by the confounding and dropout sensitivity restrictions, jointly, at zero-probability histories too. Optimizing regime values over that set would then have the right candidate range; calling the constraints closed does not prove that coincidence.
Would the confounding and dropout limits still be separately interpretable in this version?

That is the intention of retaining separate cross-product constraints: each would encode its own odds-ratio limit, one for confounding and one for dropout. They would nevertheless apply to the same admissible explanations. Separate interpretation should not be taken to mean that the constraints—or their effects on a regime value—can be analyzed independently and then combined without checking the joint feasible set.
Why use exact-binomial sets with a Bonferroni adjustment for the projection?

The proposed rationale is to obtain simultaneous protection for the observed probabilities that enter the projection. An exact-binomial confidence set can cover an individual binomial probability without relying on an interior, large-sample approximation. A Bonferroni allocation can then control the chance that any of the required individual sets misses its probability, provided the sets and allocation are specified appropriately. This is attractive when probabilities may be zero, but it remains necessary to show that the collection covers everything the projection needs.
Do the binomial probabilities have to be independent for that simultaneous argument?

No. A Bonferroni argument controls simultaneous coverage using the individual noncoverage guarantees; it does not require independence among the events. What does matter is that each individual guarantee applies to the relevant probability and that their allowed noncoverage amounts together support the desired 95% simultaneous level. The proposed construction has not specified the individual sets or their allocation yet.
How does projecting the simultaneous confidence set help with uniform coverage of the effect?

Conditionally on the simultaneous set containing the relevant observed probabilities, projection can retain every effect value compatible with those probabilities and the stated sensitivity class, if the projection is performed over the exact admissible set. To turn that observation into a uniform guarantee, the simultaneous coverage must hold uniformly over the allowed observed distributions, and the compatibility and projection argument must remain valid at zero-probability histories. This explains the proposed route to at least 95% uniform coverage; it is not itself a completed proof.
Does “exact-binomial” mean the resulting bounds are exact?

No. “Exact-binomial” concerns coverage of the component probability sets. Sharpness of the identification bounds is a separate property of the closed cross-product model and the optimization of regime values over it. Projection concerns uncertainty about observed probabilities. Even excellent coverage for those probabilities would not fix an optimization set that fails to represent the intended sensitivity class exactly.
And does the Bonferroni step necessarily produce exactly 95% coverage?

No. The aim is coverage of at least 95%, not equality to 95%. Bonferroni control and exact-binomial sets can be conservative. The relevant claim in your hypothesis is that the projected confidence region reaches at least 95% coverage uniformly, including at zero-probability histories, not that its coverage is exactly 95% everywhere.
Would a uniform guarantee at the boundary be stronger than checking each zero-probability distribution separately?

Yes. Uniformity must also account for admissible distributions whose relevant probabilities approach zero, if those distributions are in the specified sensitivity class. Verifying coverage at each fixed boundary distribution would not alone establish the required uniform asymptotic guarantee. The attraction of the proposed exact-binomial Bonferroni route is that a suitable simultaneous probability-coverage argument may avoid relying on approximations that deteriorate near the boundary; whether the full projection argument succeeds still has to be shown.
Can we state the hypothesis carefully without presenting it as a result?

Yes: hypothesize that closed cross-product constraints give an exact finite-history representation of the joint sensitivity class defined by the separate confounding and dropout odds-ratio limits, including zero-probability histories, so that optimizing regime values gives sharp bounds. Further hypothesize that projecting appropriately constructed exact-binomial confidence sets with Bonferroni simultaneous control yields confidence regions with at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly over that class. Both the boundary equivalence needed for sharpness and the uniform coverage of the projected region remain to be demonstrated.

I want to turn the zero-probability question into a plan: enumerate two-stage response types, encode separate zero-safe constraints for confounding and dropout, then prove sharpness and uniform 95% Bonferroni coverage. How should those pieces fit together?

The enumeration would define the candidate explanations over two stages and how each candidate relates to the observed information and the regime value. The two sets of zero-safe constraints would then restrict the same candidates: one set for unmeasured time-varying confounding, the other for informative dropout. The identification proof would need to show that optimizing over the resulting joint feasible set gives sharp bounds. Separately, the inference proof would need to show that a Bonferroni-based confidence-set projection has at least 95% coverage uniformly over the specified sensitivity class. Each is a planned proof obligation, not an established result.
What should enumeration accomplish beyond giving the types names?

It should make the representation sufficiently explicit that a candidate distribution over the two-stage response types determines the observed probabilities and the regime values under consideration. It should also make clear which histories enter the confounding and dropout restrictions. Enumeration is useful only if the subsequent feasible set correctly captures all admissible explanations, including those involving zero-probability histories; listing types by itself does not establish that.
Should I encode the confounding limit first and add dropout afterward?

You can describe the two restrictions separately to preserve their interpretations, but the bound must ultimately be optimized under both at once. A sequential presentation is not a justification for treating the restrictions as independent or for combining bounds obtained from two separate feasible sets. The plan is to construct their joint feasible set over the enumerated response types.
What does zero-safe mean in this plan?

It means the constraints have an explicitly defined interpretation when a relevant history has probability zero, without relying on an undefined conditional odds ratio. For each of the confounding and dropout limits, the formulation should agree with the intended odds-ratio restriction where that ratio is defined and say exactly what happens at the boundary. The zero-safe formulation is part of what the sharpness proof must check; avoiding division by zero alone is not enough.
The earlier hypothesis used closed cross-product constraints. Is the plan to prove that they are the right zero-safe encoding?

That is a natural way to formulate the proof task, while keeping the claim open. One would need to check both the positive-probability interpretation and the admissible boundary cases for each separate limit. In particular, a closed cross-product expression should not be assumed equivalent to the intended sensitivity restriction at a zero-probability history merely because it has no denominator.
How would the sharpness proof be organized?

It would need to connect the sensitivity class to the proposed two-stage feasible set in both directions. Every explanation allowed by the observed information and the separate confounding and dropout constraints must have an admissible representation in the optimization. Conversely, every feasible response-type distribution must correspond to an explanation allowed by those restrictions. If those directions hold, optimizing the relevant regime values over the joint set can establish that the resulting bounds are tight. Boundary cases are part of both directions.
Could I skip the second direction if the optimized range looks conservative?

No, not if the claim is sharpness. Including candidates the sensitivity class does not allow could make the range too wide; omitting allowed candidates could make it too narrow. A conservative outer bound would be a different claim. The planned proof must identify the exact feasible possibilities rather than rely on the appearance of the numerical extrema.
Where do the confidence sets enter?

They address uncertainty in the observed probabilities used by the identification calculation. The Bonferroni part of the plan is to secure simultaneous coverage for the probability components needed by the projection, with the total allowed noncoverage no greater than 5%. The projection would then retain effect values compatible with probabilities in that simultaneous set and with the joint sensitivity constraints. The proof still has to verify that the chosen probability sets and the projection cover the stated target.
Does the Bonferroni argument require the individual probability sets to be independent?

No. Its simultaneous noncoverage bound can be obtained by adding the individual noncoverage bounds, without independence. What the plan does require is a valid coverage statement for each component being used, an appropriate allocation of the 5% noncoverage allowance, and a projection that preserves coverage when the true observed probabilities fall in the simultaneous set.
I am especially concerned about uniformity when a history probability tends to zero. What needs to be proved there?

The confidence-set coverage and the projection argument must continue to work across admissible distributions at zero-probability histories and along admissible sequences approaching them. A proof only for fixed distributions with positive history probabilities would not give the planned uniform 95% guarantee. The inference argument also has to use the same boundary interpretation as the identification argument, so that it projects through the sensitivity class actually used to define the bounds.
Would using exact-binomial components settle that concern?

They may offer a route to probability coverage that does not depend on an interior approximation, as discussed for the Bonferroni projection. They would not, by themselves, establish sharp bounds or uniform coverage for the projected effect region. The plan still calls for checking that the component sets cover all required observed probabilities with the allocated error, that the joint coverage is uniform over the specified class, and that projection through the zero-safe feasible set preserves it.
What should I avoid claiming before completing this plan?

Avoid saying that the two-stage optimization is already sharp, that the zero-safe constraints have already been shown equivalent to the intended odds-ratio limits, or that Bonferroni projection has already achieved uniform 95% coverage. The plan is to enumerate the response types, encode the separate constraints, and prove those identification and inference properties—including at zero-probability histories.

For this activity, I want to enumerate two-stage binary response types under separate zero-safe confounding and dropout constraints, then assess 95% coverage in 10,000 structural-zero replicates. How should I keep the enumeration and coverage assessment aligned?

The enumeration should define the candidate two-stage binary response types and how distributions over them relate to observed histories and regime values. The confounding and dropout constraints should each have a stated meaning when a relevant history has probability zero, while restricting the same candidate distributions jointly. For the coverage assessment, each of the 10,000 structural-zero replicates would be evaluated using that same representation and boundary convention. This describes the activity; it does not report an enumeration or a coverage result.
What does binary qualify in “two-stage binary response types”?

It says the responses represented by the types are binary and that the representation spans two stages. It does not specify which variables are binary, the number of possible types, or the particular regime effect being evaluated. Those details would need to be defined before an exhaustive enumeration could be checked.
How do I know whether the enumeration is exhaustive?

The check is whether every response pattern permitted by the stated two-stage setup has a representation, without treating two descriptions of the same candidate as different substantive possibilities. The mapping from types to observable histories also needs to be explicit enough to evaluate the constraints and regime values. Without the particular variables and histories, there is no justified type count to give here.
Should I enumerate types separately for confounding and for dropout?

The proposed activity uses a common enumeration of candidate response types. You can state the confounding and dropout restrictions separately so each remains interpretable, but both restrict the candidate distributions used in the assessment. Two disconnected enumerations would not, on their own, describe how the mechanisms operate simultaneously.
What should zero-safe mean operationally when I encode each restriction?

Each constraint must remain well defined when a history involved in its odds-ratio interpretation has probability zero. It should also agree with the intended restriction wherever the relevant odds ratio is defined. A denominator-free form is one possible way to write a constraint, but the boundary cases must still be checked: merely avoiding an undefined calculation does not establish that the encoding represents the intended sensitivity class.
Is a structural zero just a history that happened not to appear in one replicate?

No. A structural zero means that the history has zero probability under the distribution used for that replicate. A zero observed count is a sample outcome and can occur for a history with positive probability. The distinction matters both when applying the zero-safe constraints and when interpreting the coverage assessment.
Why focus the 10,000 replicates on structural zeros?

They directly exercise the boundary behavior that motivates zero-safe constraints. An assessment based on those replicates can reveal how the proposed calculations behave when some histories truly have probability zero. It cannot, by itself, show how they behave over every distribution in the sensitivity class or prove a uniform coverage claim.
What would assessing 95% coverage mean across the replicates?

For a clearly specified inferential target, it would mean determining in each replicate whether the constructed confidence region covers that target, then summarizing the coverage frequency across the 10,000 replicates. The 95% is the coverage level being assessed, not an observed result. The activity does not yet specify the particular target or report how many regions cover it.
Could I just check whether a confidence region contains a single regime-effect value?

Only if that value is the stated target of the confidence region. The identification problem concerns a range of regime-effect values compatible with the sensitivity constraints, so the coverage event must be defined consistently with whatever the region is intended to cover. Otherwise a reported coverage frequency would answer a different question. The current activity does not settle that choice.
If the measured coverage is close to 95%, would the activity establish uniform 95% coverage?

No. A coverage frequency from 10,000 structural-zero replicates is an empirical assessment for the distributions represented in those replicates. Uniform coverage is a guarantee over the specified sensitivity class, including admissible boundary and near-boundary cases. A simulation result can inform that question but cannot replace its coverage argument.
Would the same assessment establish that the optimized bounds are sharp?

No. Sharpness concerns whether the feasible set defined by the response types and the two zero-safe constraints contains exactly the explanations allowed by the assumptions. Coverage across replicates concerns the behavior of a confidence-region procedure. Keeping those questions separate prevents favorable coverage in the structural-zero assessment from being mistaken for a proof of sharp identification.
What if one of the two constraints becomes vacuous at a structural-zero history?

That might be the intended boundary interpretation, or it might admit candidates that the intended odds-ratio restriction would not allow. The answer depends on the precise zero-safe definition. For this activity, the important check is that any vacuity or remaining restriction at a zero-probability history follows from the stated confounding or dropout sensitivity condition, rather than arising accidentally from the algebra.
Is there a way to state the scope of this activity without implying results we do not have?

Yes: enumerate the two-stage binary response types, formulate separate confounding and dropout constraints that are defined at zero-probability histories, and assess the coverage of a 95% confidence-region procedure in 10,000 structural-zero replicates. That states what is being undertaken without asserting that the bounds are sharp or that the procedure has achieved 95% coverage, uniformly or otherwise.

There is now a TwoStageZeroSafe repository containing enumerated response types, constrained optimizers, and coverage summaries from 10,000 structural-zero replicates. How should I describe what this artifact contains?

Describe it as a repository that brings together those three components: the enumerated response types for the two-stage setting, constrained optimizers for the corresponding bound calculations, and coverage summaries from 10,000 structural-zero replicates. That identifies the artifact without assigning numerical findings to the summaries or claiming that the optimizers establish sharpness.
Can I say the response types are the two-stage binary ones we have been discussing?

Yes. That identifies which response types the enumeration concerns. It does not, by itself, specify how many types were enumerated or establish that the enumeration exhausts every admissible explanation under the sensitivity constraints.
And how should I connect the constrained optimizers to confounding and dropout?

You can identify them as the optimizers associated with the two-stage formulation under separate zero-safe confounding and dropout constraints. The distinction between the constraints matters: they address different sources of uncertainty, even though an optimizer for the proposed joint bounds must account for both. The fact that constrained optimizers are in the repository does not alone establish that their feasible set is an exact representation of the intended sensitivity class.
Does “zero-safe” in that description mean zero-probability histories have been resolved?

It means the formulation is intended to handle those histories without relying on undefined odds ratios. The repository's existence does not by itself prove that the boundary interpretation of each constraint agrees exactly with the intended confounding or dropout limit. That distinction is important if you describe the artifact without making an unsupported sharpness claim.
What can I say about the coverage summaries?

They summarize the coverage assessment across 10,000 structural-zero replicates. You can state the replicate count and the structural-zero setting. Without the reported values, you cannot say what coverage was observed or whether it reached the 95% level being assessed.
Is it fair to distinguish a structural zero from an empty observed cell when describing those summaries?

Yes. A structural-zero history has zero probability under the distribution in question; a history can also have a zero count in a replicate despite having positive probability. Referring to the summaries as coming from structural-zero replicates preserves that distinction without asserting anything about their numerical outcomes.
If the repository contains both optimizers and coverage summaries, does that make it a validation of the bound and inference claims?

Not by itself. The optimizers are an artifact of the proposed identification calculation, and the summaries report an empirical coverage assessment. Sharpness requires an argument that the constrained feasible set exactly matches the stipulated sensitivity class. Uniform coverage of at least 95% requires a guarantee over that class; summaries from 10,000 replicates alone cannot supply it.
Could I call the coverage summaries a uniform-coverage result if the replicates include structural zeros?

No. Including structural zeros makes the summaries pertinent to an important boundary case, but uniformity concerns all distributions in the specified sensitivity class, including relevant near-boundary sequences. The artifact description establishes that coverage summaries exist for 10,000 structural-zero replicates, not that they prove uniform 95% coverage.
What about calling the optimizer outputs sharp bounds?

That would require more than the presence of constrained optimizers in TwoStageZeroSafe. To call their extrema sharp, one must establish that every admissible explanation is represented and that every represented candidate is admissible, including at zero-probability histories. The artifact description does not state that this has been proved.
Can you give me a concise repository description that stays within what is known?

“TwoStageZeroSafe is a repository containing enumerated two-stage binary response types, constrained optimizers for the separate zero-safe confounding and dropout formulation, and coverage summaries from 10,000 structural-zero replicates.” This describes the contents without assigning a coverage value or claiming sharpness or uniform coverage.

I want to audit TwoStageZeroSafe against exhaustive response-type bounds and estimate the minimum coverage of its 95% intervals across the 10,000 structural-zero replicates. What exactly is being evaluated?

The audit has two parts. The bound comparison checks the constrained optimizers in TwoStageZeroSafe against bounds obtained from an exhaustive response-type calculation. The coverage assessment uses its 10,000 structural-zero replicates to estimate the lowest coverage associated with the nominal 95% intervals, once the cases over which that minimum is taken are defined. Together, these checks evaluate the repository and bear on the proposed sharp-bounds and coverage claims; they do not, by themselves, report an outcome or establish uniform coverage.
What should the comparison to exhaustive response-type bounds look for?

It should compare the lower and upper bounds for the same regime effect under the same observed information and sensitivity restrictions. Agreement would be informative only if the exhaustive calculation and the repository optimizer are genuinely evaluating the same admissible set, including the separate confounding and dropout constraints at zero-probability histories. A mismatch would call for investigation, but the current activity states no comparison result.
Does calling those bounds exhaustive mean we already know they are sharp?

No. “Exhaustive response-type bounds” identifies the comparison calculation. To use it as a sharpness benchmark, one would still need to know that the exhaustive enumeration captures all and only the explanations allowed by the stated sensitivity class. The audit can compare computations without assuming that its benchmark has already proved the underlying identification claim.
Why is the boundary interpretation important in an audit of the optimizers?

The activity concerns structural-zero replicates, so zero-probability histories are directly relevant. If the optimizer and the exhaustive response-type calculation treat such histories differently, their bounds could differ for reasons unrelated to numerical optimization. The comparison needs a common interpretation of the confounding and dropout constraints before agreement or disagreement can be read as evidence about the optimizer.
What does “minimum 95% interval coverage” mean here? An individual replicate's interval either covers or it doesn't.

Right. The minimum should not be taken over individual zero-or-one coverage indicators and then described as a coverage probability. Could we use support-stratified additive-bias caps for treatment and dropout, optimize over shared full-data laws, and project exact multinomial confidence sets to study dynamic treatment-regime effects?

Why keep a treatment cap and a dropout cap separate?

They address different sources of uncertainty. The treatment cap is meant to restrict bias associated with treatment assignment and unmeasured confounding; the dropout cap is meant to restrict bias associated with informative loss of observation. Stating each separately makes its interpretation explicit. A full-data law used for the effect calculation would still have to satisfy both at once.
Does “additive” mean I can add the two caps together and impose only one combined limit?

No. “Additive-bias” describes the proposed form of each deviation; it does not say that the treatment and dropout allowances can be pooled or traded against one another. What work do the support strata do?

They make explicit which histories have the support needed to interpret a given bias comparison and how admissibility is defined at other histories. That matters when a history has zero probability or no retention: a formula conditioned on that history may not be determined there. Stratification is a way to state the applicable rule rather than silently treating an undefined comparison as zero, unrestricted, or grounds for excluding a law.
Would zero retention automatically remove a history from the optimization?

No. A history can have positive mass even if retention at that history is zero. The support-stratified formulation would need to say which full-data laws associated with such a history are admissible under the proposed dropout cap. It should not exclude a law solely because its conditional comparison cannot be evaluated, or admit every latent completion without an explicit rule.
Does an additive cap itself solve the boundary question?

Not automatically. An additive expression may avoid some undefined ratios, but a difference between conditional quantities still requires those quantities to be defined. Even a difference written in joint masses needs a stated interpretation and reference. The proposal needs support-specific admissibility rules that match the intended treatment and dropout sensitivity limits.
Why optimize shared full-data laws instead of separate treatment and dropout explanations?

The regime effect, observed information, and both bias restrictions must be compatible within one underlying law. Separate explanations might each satisfy their own cap without being jointly realizable. A shared full-data law makes the joint requirement explicit: the same candidate supplies the regime value, the observed-data implications, and the treatment and dropout quantities being constrained.
Is a shared full-data law enough to show the resulting bounds are sharp?

No. The formulation must include every law allowed by the observed information and the two support-stratified caps, and it must exclude every law those conditions forbid. If that correspondence is established, optimizing the specified regime effect over the class gives its tight identified bounds. One must also say whether a reported endpoint is attained by a law or is an infimum or supremum approached by admissible laws.

The proposed calculation takes the lowest and highest compatible values over the shared-law class. Start with a confidence set for the observed multinomial probabilities.
